```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
## Chunks that download from Synapse run only when a token is available.
have_token <- nzchar(Sys.getenv("SYNAPSE_AUTH_TOKEN"))
fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
pct <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(round(100 * x, digits), "%")
## An analysis result quoted in the prose: `value` when the Synapse steps
## ran, `otherwise` (text that does not depend on them) when they did not.
## `value` is only evaluated when there is a token.
result <- function(value, otherwise = "") {
    if (have_token) value else otherwise
}
code_list <- function(x) paste0("`", x, "`", collapse = ", ")
```

Package: [*HTAN*](https://bioconductor.org/packages/HTAN)
`r packageVersion("HTAN")`
([source](https://github.com/seandavi/HTAN)).

This vignette follows one HTAN dataset from a metadata query to a
biological result. It picks a small open spatial transcriptomics section
of the colon, confirms where it came from, downloads it, reads it into a
`SpatialExperiment`, wraps it with clinical data in a
`MultiAssayExperiment`, and runs a short analysis: quality control,
normalisation, clustering and spatial plots. Along the way it explains why
each step is done the way it is.

It assumes the [introduction](HTAN.html) and the
[data model vignette](data-model.html). The metadata steps run anywhere.
The download, and every step after it, needs a free Synapse account and a
personal access token in `SYNAPSE_AUTH_TOKEN` (see the introduction), so
where the vignette is built without a token, for example on the
Bioconductor build machines, that code is shown without being run.

```{r}
#| label: packages
#| warning: false
library(SpatialExperiment)
library(scater)
library(scrapper)
library(HTAN)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
con <- htan_con("r7")
```

The order matters: the Bioconductor packages attach functions named
`count()`, `desc()`, `slice()` and `rename()` that mask dplyr's, so dplyr
is attached last.

# Choosing a dataset

## The question

The Vanderbilt atlas (HTA11) studied colorectal precancer and cancer. A
section of colon is a good first spatial dataset. The colonic mucosa has
an obvious architecture (epithelial crypts, the stroma of the lamina
propria, immune cells), so the expression clusters of a correct analysis
can be checked against recognisable tissue compartments, and against what
the metadata say the tissue is.

## Finding candidate files

10x Visium measures the transcriptome in a grid of 55 µm spots across a
tissue section. Level 4 Visium files are processed objects, ready to
analyse. Here are the open ones:

```{r}
#| label: visium-candidates
visium <- htan_files(
    assay == "10xVisiumSpatialTranscriptomics-RNA-seq", level == 4,
    access == "open-synapse", con = con)
visium |>
    count(HTAN_Center, extension) |>
    arrange(desc(n)) |>
    collect()
```

Three things guide the choice. First, the format: `.h5ad` (AnnData) files
follow a common layout that anndataR reads reliably, whereas `.rds` files
hold whatever R object the center saved. Second, provenance: a file from a
single participant, measured on a biospecimen whose tissue type and site
are recorded, so the result can be read against them. Third, size: small
enough to download in seconds. The biospecimen fields come from the
`biospecimen` table, joined on the assayed biospecimen:

```{r}
#| label: candidates
biospecimens <- htan_tbl("biospecimen", con) |>
    select(HTAN_Assayed_Biospecimen_ID = HTAN_Biospecimen_ID,
        Tumor_Tissue_Type, Site_of_Resection_or_Biopsy)
candidates <- visium |>
    filter(extension == ".h5ad", n_participants == 1) |>
    inner_join(biospecimens, by = "HTAN_Assayed_Biospecimen_ID") |>
    filter(Tumor_Tissue_Type != "Not Otherwise Specified",
        Site_of_Resection_or_Biopsy != "Not Reported") |>
    arrange(File_Size) |>
    select(HTAN_Data_File_ID, Filename, File_Size, Tumor_Tissue_Type,
        Site_of_Resection_or_Biopsy) |>
    collect()
nrow(candidates)
candidates |>
    transmute(file = basename(Filename), MB = round(File_Size / 1e6),
        Tumor_Tissue_Type, site = Site_of_Resection_or_Biopsy) |>
    head(10)
```

One property that matters is not in the metadata: the version of AnnData
that wrote each file. Files written before AnnData 0.8 (released in 2022)
use an older on-disk layout that anndataR does not read. `read_htan()`
reads those with a fallback that keeps the matrices, `obs`, `var` and
`obsm`, but not `uns`. Every file smaller than
`7794_AS_3_unfiltered.h5ad` in this list is in that older layout (checked
by opening each one), so this vignette uses `7794_AS_3`, the smallest file
in the current layout, which anndataR reads in full:

```{r}
#| label: pick
visium_id <- "HTA11_99999933430_8422134111"
stopifnot(visium_id %in% candidates$HTAN_Data_File_ID)
file <- htan_files(HTAN_Data_File_ID == visium_id, con = con) |> collect()
glimpse(select(file, HTAN_Data_File_ID, Filename, File_Size, md5,
    entityId, HTAN_Participant_ID, HTAN_Assayed_Biospecimen_ID, access))
```

The `entityId` is its Synapse ID; `access` is `open-synapse`, so a token is
needed but no data access request.

## What the metadata say about it

The assay table holds the processing details:

```{r}
#| label: workflow
workflow <- htan_tbl(
    "10xvisium_spatialtranscriptomics_scRNAseq_level4_metadata", con) |>
    filter(HTAN_Data_File_ID == visium_id) |>
    select(Workflow_Version, Visium_Workflow_Type,
        Visium_Workflow_Parameters_Description, Run_ID, Data_Release) |>
    collect()
glimpse(workflow)
```

The file was made with Space Ranger against the GRCh38-2020-A reference,
with the human whole-transcriptome probe set, so this is the probe-based
Visium chemistry. The record disagrees with itself about the Space Ranger
version (`Workflow_Version` is `r workflow$Workflow_Version`, but
`Visium_Workflow_Type` says `r workflow$Visium_Workflow_Type`): these
fields were filled in by hand at submission, and are worth reading
sceptically. "Unfiltered" in the file name suggests it holds every spot
on the capture area, not only those under tissue, which the analysis will
need to handle.

# Tracing lineage

Before using a processed file, check what it was made from:

```{r}
#| label: lineage
lineage <- htan_lineage(visium_id, con = con) |>
    arrange(depth, related_file_id) |>
    collect()
lineage |>
    transmute(depth, Component = sub("10xVisiumSpatialTranscriptomics-",
        "", Component), file = basename(Filename))
```

FASTQ (Level 1, controlled), aligned BAM (Level 2, controlled), the Space
Ranger output (Level 3, open) and this object (Level 4). All were measured
on one biospecimen. Its record, and the participant's:

```{r}
#| label: biospecimen
biospecimen <- htan_tbl("biospecimen", con) |>
    filter(HTAN_Biospecimen_ID == !!file$HTAN_Assayed_Biospecimen_ID) |>
    select(HTAN_Biospecimen_ID, HTAN_Parent_ID, Acquisition_Method_Type,
        Preservation_Method, Tumor_Tissue_Type, Site_of_Resection_or_Biopsy,
        Histologic_Morphology_Code) |>
    collect()
glimpse(biospecimen)

htan_tbl("clinical_tier1_demographics", con) |>
    filter(HTAN_Participant_ID == !!file$HTAN_Participant_ID) |>
    select(HTAN_Participant_ID, Gender, Race, Vital_Status) |>
    collect()

diagnosis <- htan_tbl("clinical_tier1_diagnosis", con) |>
    filter(HTAN_Participant_ID == !!file$HTAN_Participant_ID) |>
    select(Primary_Diagnosis, Morphology, Tissue_or_Organ_of_Origin,
        Tumor_Grade) |>
    collect()
diagnosis
```

The section is a `r tolower(biospecimen$Acquisition_Method_Type)` of the
`r tolower(biospecimen$Site_of_Resection_or_Biopsy)`, with tissue type
"`r biospecimen$Tumor_Tissue_Type`", HTAN's term for tissue from a primary
tumour (as opposed to premalignant, normal or metastatic tissue). Nothing
more specific is recorded: the morphology code is
`r biospecimen$Histologic_Morphology_Code` (not reported), and the
participant's primary diagnosis is "`r diagnosis$Primary_Diagnosis`".
So the metadata do not say whether the lesion is an adenoma or a
carcinoma, or of what type; the analysis has to be read without that.
The participant has other data too, which could extend this analysis
later:

```{r}
#| label: other-data
htan_files(participants = file$HTAN_Participant_ID, con = con) |>
    count(Component, access) |>
    arrange(Component) |>
    collect()
```

# Downloading

`htan_download()` checks the access tier and total size, asks Synapse for
a short-lived download URL, fetches the file, and verifies its md5 against
the metadata. The file is kept in the package's download cache (a
BiocFileCache under `tools::R_user_dir("HTAN", "cache")`), so a second
call finds the verified copy and does not download again. Pass `dest` to
also copy files to a directory of your choice.

```{r}
#| label: download
#| eval: !expr have_token
dl <- htan_download(file, con = con)
dl
```

# Reading into a SpatialExperiment

`read_htan()` reads `.h5ad` files with anndataR. When the AnnData object
has a `spatial` embedding (the layout scanpy writes for Visium), the result
is a `SpatialExperiment` with the spot positions as `spatialCoords()`:

```{r}
#| label: read
#| eval: !expr have_token
spe <- read_htan(dl)
spe
```

Level 4 objects differ between centers, so look before you compute. Three
things matter here: which assay holds raw counts, whether there are spot
coordinates, and which spots are under tissue.

```{r}
#| label: inspect
#| eval: !expr have_token
assayNames(spe)
names(colData(spe))
names(rowData(spe))
head(rownames(spe))
is(spe, "SpatialExperiment")
```

Marker genes are easier to read as symbols. If the row names are Ensembl
IDs, use a symbol column from `rowData()` instead (scanpy and Space Ranger
call it different things), keeping names unique. Some probe-set features
are named `DEPRECATED_` followed by an Ensembl ID; they are counted here
and left as they are.

```{r}
#| label: symbols
#| eval: !expr have_token
if (mean(grepl("^ENSG", rownames(spe))) > 0.5) {
    symbol_col <- intersect(c("gene_symbols", "gene_name", "feature_name",
        "symbol", "gene_ids"), names(rowData(spe)))[1]
    rownames(spe) <- make.unique(as.character(rowData(spe)[[symbol_col]]))
}
head(rownames(spe))
sum(grepl("^DEPRECATED_", rownames(spe)))
```

anndataR maps AnnData's main matrix `X` to an assay named `X`. Whether `X`
is raw counts or normalised values is the center's choice, so test it: raw
counts are whole numbers.

```{r}
#| label: counts
#| eval: !expr have_token
x <- assay(spe, "X")
sample_values <- as.numeric(x[, seq_len(min(200, ncol(x)))])
all(sample_values == round(sample_values))
assay(spe, "counts") <- x
assay(spe, "X") <- NULL
```

If this were `FALSE`, the counts would have to come from a layer of the
AnnData object or from the Level 3 Space Ranger matrix listed in the
lineage.

If the object had no spatial embedding, the spot positions are in the
Level 3 `tissue_positions.csv` from the lineage table, which can be
downloaded and joined by barcode. This chunk does that only when needed:

```{r}
#| label: coordinates
#| eval: !expr have_token
if (!is(spe, "SpatialExperiment")) {
    pos_id <- lineage$related_file_id[
        grepl("tissue_positions", lineage$Filename)]
    pos_dl <- htan_download(pos_id, con = con)
    ## Space Ranger 2.0 writes a header row; 1.x did not.
    has_header <- startsWith(readLines(pos_dl$path, n = 1), "barcode")
    pos <- read.csv(pos_dl$path, header = has_header)
    names(pos) <- c("barcode", "in_tissue", "array_row", "array_col",
        "pxl_row", "pxl_col")
    pos <- pos[match(colnames(spe), pos$barcode), ]
    colData(spe)$in_tissue <- pos$in_tissue
    spe <- as(spe, "SpatialExperiment")
    spatialCoords(spe) <- as.matrix(pos[, c("pxl_col", "pxl_row")])
}
dim(spatialCoords(spe))
```

Finally, keep only spots under tissue. Spots outside the tissue capture
ambient RNA and would form their own spurious cluster:

```{r}
#| label: in-tissue
#| eval: !expr have_token
if ("in_tissue" %in% names(colData(spe))) {
    print(table(in_tissue = spe$in_tissue))
    spe <- spe[, spe$in_tissue == 1]
}
dim(spe)
```

# Adding clinical context: a MultiAssayExperiment

`htan_experiment()` builds a `MultiAssayExperiment` from objects named by
their `HTAN_Data_File_ID`. It looks up each file's participant in
`id_provenance`, maps every spot to that participant in the `sampleMap`,
and fills `colData` with the participant's demographics and diagnosis.
Biospecimen annotation is per sample rather than per participant, so it is
added to the spots' own `colData` first:

```{r}
#| label: mae
#| eval: !expr have_token
for (field in c("HTAN_Biospecimen_ID", "Tumor_Tissue_Type",
    "Site_of_Resection_or_Biopsy", "Histologic_Morphology_Code")) {
    colData(spe)[[field]] <- biospecimen[[field]]
}
mae <- htan_experiment(setNames(list(spe), visium_id), con = con)
mae
MultiAssayExperiment::colData(mae)[, c("Gender", "Race", "Vital_Status",
    "Primary_Diagnosis")]
head(MultiAssayExperiment::sampleMap(mae))
```

With one file the container is small, but the structure is the point:
adding the participant's single-cell data, or other participants' Visium
sections, keeps every spot and cell linked to one clinical record. For a
file pooled from several participants, `htan_experiment()` needs the
`colData` column that names each cell's participant
(`participant_col`); see the [data model vignette](data-model.html#a-file-from-several-participants).

The analysis below works on the `SpatialExperiment` itself:

```{r}
#| label: get-experiment
#| eval: !expr have_token
spe <- MultiAssayExperiment::experiments(mae)[[1]]
```

# Analysis

The steps follow the standard Bioconductor workflow for spot-based
spatial transcriptomics, as in the book *Orchestrating Spatial Transcriptomics
Analysis with Bioconductor* ([OSTA](https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OSTA/))
and its single-cell counterpart
([scrapbook](https://bioconductor.org/books/release/scrapbook/)), with
choices explained as they come. Like both books, it computes with
[scrapper](https://bioconductor.org/packages/scrapper/), which implements
the methods of scran and scuttle in C++ libraries (libscran) shared with
the Python and JavaScript ports, and plots with scater. Each scrapper
function ending in `.se` takes a `SummarizedExperiment` (here the
`SpatialExperiment`) and returns it with its results added.

## Quality control

Per-spot metrics: total counts (library size) and the number of genes
detected. In most RNA data a third metric is the share of counts from the
mitochondrially encoded genes (`MT-` genes), which rises in damaged
cells. A probe-based assay only measures the genes its panel targets,
unlike poly(A) capture, which picks up whatever transcripts are present,
and the panel used for this section has no probes for the `MT-` genes. So
the code looks for them, and adds the mitochondrial share only if there
are any. (Genes such as `MTRNR2L12` are nuclear, despite the name, and the
`^MT-` pattern rightly skips them.)

```{r}
#| label: qc
#| eval: !expr have_token
is_mito <- grepl("^MT-", rownames(spe), ignore.case = TRUE)
sum(is_mito)
qc_subsets <- if (any(is_mito)) list(mito = is_mito) else list()
spe <- quickRnaQc.se(spe, subsets = qc_subsets)
summary(spe$sum)
summary(spe$detected)
if (any(is_mito)) summary(spe$subset.proportion.mito)
```

Plotting the metrics on the tissue (image row coordinates increase
downwards, hence the reversed y axis) shows whether low-quality spots are
scattered (technical) or form a region (biological):

```{r}
#| label: fig-qc
#| eval: !expr have_token
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Library size of each spot under tissue."
spot_coords <- function(spe) {
    xy <- as.data.frame(spatialCoords(spe))
    names(xy) <- c("x", "y")
    xy
}
spot_plot <- function(spe, values, name) {
    ggplot(cbind(spot_coords(spe), value = values),
        aes(x, y, colour = value)) +
        geom_point(size = 1) +
        scale_y_reverse() +
        coord_fixed() +
        labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = name) +
        theme_void()
}
spot_plot(spe, log10(spe$sum + 1), "log10\ncounts") +
    scale_colour_viridis_c()
```

Spots are flagged as outliers by median absolute deviations (MADs) from
the median, instead of fixed thresholds, because sensible thresholds depend
on the tissue, the probe panel and sequencing depth. `quickRnaQc.se()`
has already done this: it set each threshold three MADs from the median,
testing library size and detected genes on the low side only (and the
mitochondrial share, when there is one, on the high side), and stored the
verdict in `keep`. The thresholds are kept in the object's metadata:

```{r}
#| label: qc-filter
#| eval: !expr have_token
thresholds <- metadata(spe)$qc$thresholds
unlist(thresholds)
n_before <- ncol(spe)
n_discard <- sum(!spe$keep)
c(low_sum = sum(spe$sum < thresholds$sum),
    low_detected = sum(spe$detected < thresholds$detected),
    discard = n_discard)
spe <- spe[, spe$keep]
dim(spe)
```

A large discarded fraction, or discarded spots forming a region, would
call for a closer look before dropping them`r result(paste0("; here ",
fmt(n_discard), " of the ", fmt(n_before), " spots ",
if (n_discard == 1) "is" else "are", " discarded"))`.

## Normalisation

Spots differ in library size for technical reasons (capture efficiency,
tissue thickness) and biological ones (cell density). Library-size
normalisation followed by a log transform is the usual choice for Visium.
The pooling-based size factors common in single-cell work assume most
genes are not differentially expressed between pools of cells, which is
less safe for spots that mix several cells of different types.
`normalizeRnaCounts.se()` uses the library sizes as size factors by
default, scaled to average 1, and adds the `logcounts` assay.

```{r}
#| label: normalise
#| eval: !expr have_token
spe <- normalizeRnaCounts.se(spe)
summary(spe$sizeFactor)
```

## Feature selection and dimensionality reduction

Highly variable genes carry the structure; the rest add noise. The variance
of each gene's log-expression is modelled against its mean, and the 2,000
genes with the largest residual above that trend are marked in
`rowData(spe)$hvg`. Where there are mitochondrial genes, they are then
removed from the set so that tissue damage does not drive the clustering;
this panel has none, so here the step does nothing.

```{r}
#| label: hvgs
#| eval: !expr have_token
spe <- chooseRnaHvgs.se(spe, top = 2000)
if (any(is_mito)) {
    rowData(spe)$hvg <- rowData(spe)$hvg & !is_mito
}
sum(rowData(spe)$hvg)
hvg_stats <- rowData(spe)[rowData(spe)$hvg, ]
head(rownames(hvg_stats)[order(hvg_stats$residuals, decreasing = TRUE)], 20)
```

```{r}
#| label: pca
#| eval: !expr have_token
spe <- runPca.se(spe, features = rowData(spe)$hvg, number = 30)
pca <- metadata(spe)$PCA
percent_var <- 100 * pca$variance.explained / pca$total.variance
round(head(percent_var, 10), 1)
```

Thirty components are kept, a common default that is generous for a
tissue with a handful of domains. No single component explains much of
the variance`r result(paste0(" (the first ", round(percent_var[1], 1),
"%, the second ", round(percent_var[2], 1), "%)"))`, which is usual for
spots that each average several cells.

## Clustering

Spots are clustered on the principal components with a shared
nearest-neighbour graph (Jaccard-weighted) and the Leiden algorithm at
resolution 0.5, the settings OSTA uses for its colorectal Visium workflow.
This uses expression alone; the spatial plot afterwards is then a test:
if clusters computed without coordinates form coherent regions, they
reflect real tissue structure. Spatially aware methods (for example
BayesSpace or Banksy) smooth over neighbours and would give cleaner
domains, at the cost of that independent check.

```{r}
#| label: cluster
#| eval: !expr have_token
spe <- clusterGraph.se(spe, method = "leiden", resolution = 0.5,
    more.build.args = list(weight.scheme = "jaccard"),
    output.name = "cluster")
table(spe$cluster)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-clusters
#| eval: !expr have_token
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Expression clusters on the tissue section."
spot_plot(spe, spe$cluster, "Cluster") +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-umap
#| eval: !expr have_token
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "UMAP of spots, coloured by cluster."
spe <- runUmap.se(spe)
plotReducedDim(spe, "UMAP", colour_by = "cluster")
```

## What the clusters are

Marker genes say what each cluster is. `scoreMarkers.se()` compares each
cluster with every other one and summarises the pairwise effect sizes for
each gene: Cohen's d (the difference in mean log-expression in standard
deviations), the AUC (the probability that a spot in the cluster has
higher expression than a spot in the other), and the differences in mean
expression and in the proportion of spots where the gene is detected.
Genes are ranked by Cohen's d averaged over the comparisons. Effect sizes
are a better summary than p-values here: the clusters were defined from
these same expression values, so a test for differences between them is
circular and its p-values would not mean what they usually do.

```{r}
#| label: markers
#| eval: !expr have_token
markers <- scoreMarkers.se(spe, groups = spe$cluster)
top_markers <- vapply(markers, function(m) {
    paste(head(rownames(m), 8), collapse = ", ")
}, "")
tibble::tibble(cluster = names(top_markers), top_markers = top_markers)
```

Some clusters are led by members of multi-copy gene families, such as
`SERF1A` and `SERF1B`, `FAM153B`, the `USP17L` genes and `MTRNR2L12`,
rather than by genes that mark a cell type. Each of these families has
several near-identical copies in the genome, so a probe, or a read, may
not be specific to one of them; the `MTRNR2L` genes are also close copies
of the mitochondrial rRNA gene `MT-RNR2`. Their signal may therefore be
partly technical (this is unverified). A per-cluster summary makes the
pattern easier to see: the number of spots, their median depth, the
median share of each spot's counts that goes to these families, and the
mean log-expression of an epithelial and a stromal marker.

```{r}
#| label: cluster-summary
#| eval: !expr have_token
multicopy <- grepl("^(SERF1|USP17L|FAM153|MTRNR2L|TAF11L|GAGE|CT45A)",
    rownames(spe))
sum(multicopy)
clusters <- factor(spe$cluster)
per_cluster <- function(v, f = median) as.vector(tapply(v, clusters, f))
cluster_summary <- tibble::tibble(
    cluster = levels(clusters),
    spots = per_cluster(spe$sum, length),
    median_counts = per_cluster(spe$sum),
    median_genes = per_cluster(spe$detected),
    multicopy_share = round(per_cluster(
        colSums(counts(spe)[multicopy, ]) / spe$sum), 2),
    EPCAM = round(per_cluster(logcounts(spe)["EPCAM", ], mean), 2),
    COL1A1 = round(per_cluster(logcounts(spe)["COL1A1", ], mean), 2)
)
cluster_summary
epi <- cluster_summary$cluster[which.max(cluster_summary$EPCAM)]
stroma <- cluster_summary$cluster[which.max(cluster_summary$COL1A1)]
shallow <- cluster_summary$cluster[which.min(cluster_summary$median_counts)]
deepest <- cluster_summary$cluster[which.max(cluster_summary$median_counts)]
```

The top of the ranking for the most epithelial cluster (highest mean
`EPCAM`) shows the statistics behind it: mean log-expression and detected
proportion in the cluster, then the mean Cohen's d and AUC against the
other clusters.

```{r}
#| label: markers-epithelial
#| eval: !expr have_token
previewMarkers(markers[[epi]], rows = 8, columns = c("mean", "detected",
    d = "cohens.d.mean", auc = "auc.mean"))
```

Known markers of the colonic mucosa make the interpretation concrete:
`EPCAM` for epithelium, `MUC2` for goblet cells and their mucin, `CA1` for
the absorptive colonocytes that line normal colonic epithelium, `COL1A1`
for stroma and `PTPRC` for immune cells. `SERF1A` stands in for the
multi-copy families. Their expression levels differ widely, so each gene
is coloured relative to its own maximum:

```{r}
#| label: fig-genes
#| eval: !expr have_token
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-cap: "Marker genes on the tissue, each relative to its maximum."
genes <- intersect(c("EPCAM", "MUC2", "CA1", "COL1A1", "PTPRC", "SERF1A"),
    rownames(spe))
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(genes, function(g) {
    v <- logcounts(spe)[g, ]
    cbind(spot_coords(spe), gene = g, relative = v / max(v))
}))
ggplot(long, aes(x, y, colour = relative)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6) +
    scale_colour_viridis_c(labels = scales::percent) +
    scale_y_reverse() +
    coord_fixed() +
    facet_wrap(~ gene) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = "Share of\nmaximum") +
    theme_void()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cluster-genes
#| eval: !expr have_token
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Marker expression by cluster."
plotDots(spe, features = genes, group = "cluster")
```

```{r}
#| label: interpretation
#| eval: !expr have_token
#| include: false
detected_in <- function(g) mean(counts(spe)[g, ] > 0)
colonocyte <- intersect(c("CA1", "FABP1", "SLC26A3", "AQP8"), rownames(spe))
colonocyte_max <- max(vapply(colonocyte, detected_in, 0))
cluster_n <- function(k) paste("cluster", k)
top_genes <- function(k, n = 6) code_list(head(rownames(markers[[k]]), n))
share <- function(k) {
    pct(cluster_summary$multicopy_share[cluster_summary$cluster == k])
}
```

Read together, the plots and the summary suggest three kinds of spot.

- **Epithelium.** The cluster with the highest `EPCAM`
  `r result(paste0("(", cluster_n(epi), ") "))`has epithelial and
  secretory genes among its top markers`r result(paste0(" (",
  top_genes(epi, 8), ")", if (epi == deepest) ", and the deepest spots"))`.
- **Stroma.** The cluster with the highest `COL1A1`
  `r result(paste0("(", cluster_n(stroma), ") "))`is led by collagens and
  other stromal and extracellular-matrix genes`r result(paste0(" (",
  top_genes(stroma), ")"))`.
- **Shallow spots.** The cluster with the fewest counts per spot
  `r result(paste0("(", cluster_n(shallow), ") "))`is led by the multi-copy
  families`r result(paste0(" (", top_genes(shallow), ")"))`, which take
  `r result(share(shallow), "a large share")` of a typical spot's counts
  there. It lies along the edges of the section, where the library-size
  map is darkest, and may reflect capture depth more than a cell type.

The section as a whole does not look like normal colonic mucosa. `MUC2`
is detected throughout`r result(paste0(" (in ",
pct(detected_in("MUC2")), " of spots)"))`, while the markers of absorptive
colonocytes (`r code_list(c("CA1", "FABP1", "SLC26A3", "AQP8"))`) are
almost absent`r result(paste0(" (each detected in at most ",
pct(colonocyte_max), " of spots)"))`, and so is the immune marker
`PTPRC``r result(paste0(" (", pct(detected_in("PTPRC")), ")"))`. That
would fit a mucin-rich lesion, but the histology is not recorded, so it
remains a hypothesis: the H&E image of the section (an auxiliary file of a
few gigabytes) is the place to check it.

So the expression clusters do form regions on the tissue, which suggests
real structure, but here they separate spots by depth and by a few gene
families as well as by tissue compartment. Two next steps would sharpen
them: drop the multi-copy families from the highly variable genes and
recluster, and compare the regions with the H&E image.

# Where to go from here

- **More sections.** Other Vanderbilt Visium files cover more colon
  lesions (`candidates` above). Read several, give each its file ID, and
  combine them in one `MultiAssayExperiment`; integrate them with batch
  correction (for example scrapper's `correctMnn.se()`) before joint
  clustering.
- **Single-cell reference.** The participant also has single-cell
  RNA-seq (Level 3 count matrices). Cell types from those can be used to
  deconvolve the spots (for example with
  [SPOTlight](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/SPOTlight.html)).
- **Spatial domains and statistics.**
  [BayesSpace](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/BayesSpace.html)
  or [Banksy](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/Banksy.html)
  for spatially smoothed domains;
  [nnSVG](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/nnSVG.html)
  for spatially variable genes.
- **Other participants.** `htan_files()` and the clinical tables find
  comparable sections from other atlases, for example premalignant versus
  invasive tissue.

# Notes on reproducibility

The metadata release is pinned (`htan_con("r7")`), the file is identified
by its HTAN ID and checked against its md5, and the random steps (PCA,
clustering, UMAP) use scrapper's fixed default seeds, so they give the
same result on every run without `set.seed()`, for a given platform and
set of package versions. Across versions and platforms the details can
change: builds of this vignette with different scrapper releases and
numerical libraries have given five or six clusters. That is why every
result quoted in the text above is computed from the output rather than
written in by hand. The software versions are below. What is not pinned is the file's content
on Synapse: if the center replaced it, the md5 check would fail rather than
silently give a different result.
